In 76 of the 82 the crescent comes first and the dot second; all 79 two-stroke crescents run from left to right, turning anticlockwise, and 78 put the dot above the crescent. The dot's own direction is not settled (48 of the 82 end lower than they start), so it is drawn as a short downward dab. Each sign was written by itself, with no consonant beside it, so the traces fix the sign's own strokes but not when it is written against its consonant or the headline; the book draws the sign alone and composes no Devanagari word from it. The traces are scaled to a square, so they fix the start, the direction and the pen lifts, not the proportions: the path is fitted to the bundled Noto Sans Devanagari outline of the sign on its own. The underlying HP Labs data is licensed for research use only, so only counts and shares are cited here, and no trace was copied. Handwriting varies by writer.

source.variation: The four buildup frames show four ordered pen-down runs: frame 1 starts at the upper-left and carries the upper curve into the lower bowl without lifting; frame 2 restarts at the middle junction and sweeps right through the shoulder; frame 3 descends the right stem top-to-bottom; frame 4 draws the shirorekhā left-to-right, for three intervening lifts. Thomas Egenes, Learning the Sanskrit Alphabet, p. 12 (Maharishi International University Press, 1990), documents a six-stroke traditional Sanskrit form instead. These runs stage the letter one part at a time; they are not a count of native pen lifts. The lift count follows HP Labs India's isolated handwritten Devanagari character data (hpl-dvng-iso-char, https://lipitk.sourceforge.net/datasets/dvngchardata.htm), counted from the native-writer prototypes in the MIT-licensed LipiTk 4.0 Devanagari recognizer. Those counts say how many strokes writers use, not where they break, so this learner path keeps every run's order, start and direction as a segment and joins the middle shoulder and the right stem, which already touch, climbing the stem before descending it, so the pen lifts only before the shoulder and the headline. The counts do not say which join native writers make; this is the one औ uses. Its curves are fitted to Noto Sans Devanagari.

The traces are scaled to a square, so they fix the start, the direction and the pen lifts, not the proportions: the path is fitted to the bundled Noto Sans Devanagari outline of the sign on its own.
